question: During the Second World War, Allied engineers studied bombers that returned from missions and mapped where they had been hit by enemy fire. A statistician then advised them to add armour to the parts of the aircraft that showed NO bullet holes. Why?
correct_answer: Planes hit there never came back
alternative_answers: Hits in those areas were fatal
The planes hit there were shot down
Damage in the marked areas was survivable, so the unmarked areas must be the deadly ones
The shot-down planes were missing from the data
headline_answer: Planes hit there never came back
source_excerpt: the damaged portions of returning planes show locations where they can sustain damage and still return home; those hit in other places presumedly do not survive.

extra.verification_notes: Wald's survivorship-bias reasoning matches the answer: planes hit in the unmarked areas didn't return (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Wald).

explanation: The engineers only saw the survivors. Bullet holes on the returning planes marked places where a bomber could take damage and still fly home, such as the wings and fuselage. The areas that were clean, like the engines and cockpit, were clean because any plane hit there was shot down and never made it back to be studied. The statistician Abraham Wald recognised this flaw, now known as survivorship bias, and recommended armouring the apparently untouched sections instead.

question: In June 1940, Hitler had an old railway carriage hauled out of a museum so that France could sign its surrender inside it. What had been signed in that very carriage in November 1918?
correct_answer: The Armistice ending World War One
alternative_answers: Germany's surrender in World War One
source_excerpt: On 21 June 1940, the car was removed from its museum building and placed on the exact spot it had been in 1918.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes the carriage was just a convenient venue; the twist is that Hitler chose it deliberately to reverse the humiliation of 1918.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the carriage was removed from its museum building in June 1940 and was the site of the 11 November 1918 armistice signing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compiègne_Wagon).

explanation: The carriage stood in the forest of Compiègne, where Germany had accepted defeat in 1918, and Hitler staged the 1940 ceremony there to turn that humiliation around.

question: Japanese lieutenant Hiroo Onoda kept fighting in the jungle of Lubang Island in the Philippines because no one had officially told him the war was over. In which decade did he finally surrender?
source_excerpt: Onoda surrendered on March 10, 1974, after nearly 29 years of hiding.

extra.why_interesting: Players know some soldiers held out after 1945 but assume a few years at most; the correct decade is almost three decades after the war ended.
extra.verification_notes: Onoda surrendered on March 10, 1974, which is in the 1970s; the 'never officially told' premise is a simplification (leaflets were dropped), but the answer is unambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroo_Onoda).

explanation: Onoda laid down his rifle in March 1974, nearly 29 years after Japan surrendered, and only after his former commanding officer flew out to relieve him of duty in person.

question: Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe to give women the vote in national elections. In which year did Swiss men finally approve it in a referendum?
source_excerpt: Women in Switzerland gained the right to vote in federal elections after a referendum in February 1971

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a wealthy Western democracy enfranchised women after WWI or WWII; the true year is in the era of the Moon landings.
extra.verification_notes: Swiss men approved federal women's suffrage in the February 1971 referendum (the 1959 attempt failed); no later event changes this, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Men voted it through in February 1971, more than half a century after Germany and Britain, and one canton held out on local votes until a court forced it in 1990.

question: The 1918 influenza pandemic is popularly named after a European country where it did not begin, simply because that country was neutral in the war and its newspapers reported the outbreak freely. Which country?
source_excerpt: newspapers freely reported the outbreak in neutral Spain, creating a misleading impression of Spain as the epicenter and leading to the disease being known as Spanish flu.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the nickname marks the country of origin; the real reason is wartime censorship, and neutrality is the foothold that leads to Spain.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the name arose because neutral Spain's press freely reported the outbreak, and the pandemic did not originate in Spain (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu).

explanation: Britain, France, Germany and the US censored news of the disease to protect morale, so the Spanish headlines made it look as if the illness had started there.

question: True or false: Japan and Russia have still never signed a formal peace treaty ending the Second World War.
source_excerpt: a permanent peace treaty between Japan and Russia has not been concluded

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every WWII belligerent made formal peace decades ago; the claim sounds like a trick, but it is true.
extra.verification_notes: No Japan-Russia peace treaty has been signed; talks were suspended by Russia in 2022 and relations have deteriorated through 2026 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuril_Islands_dispute).

explanation: A 1956 declaration restored diplomatic relations, but the dispute over the Kuril Islands seized by the Soviet Union in 1945 has blocked a full peace treaty ever since.

question: In November 1939, the Soviet Union attacked a small neighbour and was expelled from the League of Nations for it. Which country was invaded?
source_excerpt: The USSR invaded Finland on 30 November 1939... the League of Nations deemed the attack illegal and expelled the Soviet Union

extra.why_interesting: Players remember Poland as the 1939 victim and forget the Soviets attacked a second neighbour that winter; the expulsion detail is the surprise.
extra.verification_notes: The USSR invaded Finland on 30 Nov 1939 and was expelled from the League of Nations for it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_War).

explanation: The Winter War saw the badly outnumbered Finns hold off the Red Army for over three months, and the League's expulsion of the Soviets was one of its last meaningful acts.

question: Which of these Nordic countries stayed neutral and was never invaded or at war during the Second World War?
source_excerpt: Sweden maintained official neutrality throughout WWII and was never invaded or formally at war.

extra.why_interesting: Four Nordic neighbours look identical on the surface; the player must know which one managed to stay out of the fighting entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Sweden remained officially neutral and was never invaded or formally at war in WWII, while Norway and Denmark were invaded and Finland fought the USSR and Germany (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden_during_World_War_II).

explanation: Germany occupied Denmark and Norway in April 1940, and Finland fought two wars against the Soviet Union, while Sweden kept out by trading with both sides.

question: The 1936 Summer Olympics were turned into a showcase for the Nazi regime, famously undermined when American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals. Which city hosted those Games?
source_excerpt: The 1936 Summer Olympics...were an international multi-sport event held from 1 to 16 August 1936 in Berlin, Germany.

extra.why_interesting: Easy entry question with a clear foothold: the propaganda angle points straight to Nazi Germany's capital.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1936 Summer Olympics were held in Berlin and that Jesse Owens won four golds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics).

explanation: The Games were awarded to Germany before Hitler took power, and he used them to present a polished face to the world while Owens stole the show on the track.

question: The deadliest pandemic of the 20th century broke out in 1918. By what name is it commonly known, borrowed from a neutral country whose newspapers were simply free to report on it?
source_excerpt: Spain was a neutral country unconcerned with appearances of combat readiness

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the name marks where the disease began; in fact it only marks the one country honest enough to print the news.
extra.verification_notes: Spanish flu is named for neutral Spain's free press reporting on the 1918 pandemic; the 'deadliest of the 20th century' phrasing is conventional, with a minor HIV/AIDS caveat only. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu

explanation: Spain was neutral in the First World War, so its press covered the outbreak openly while censors in the fighting nations kept quiet, and the unfair name stuck.

question: Wojtek was officially enlisted as a private in the Polish army, had his own paybook, and hauled crates of artillery shells at Monte Cassino in 1944. What kind of animal was he?
source_excerpt: Wojtek was officially drafted into the Polish Army as a private and listed among the soldiers of the 22nd Artillery Supply Company

extra.why_interesting: An enlisted soldier with a rank and a service record turns out to be a bear; the clues about size and strength let a thoughtful player reason their way there.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear enlisted as a private with a paybook who carried shell crates at Monte Cassino; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear adopted as a cub by Polish soldiers in Iran, and he spent his retirement at Edinburgh Zoo, where former comrades came to visit him.

question: In 1943 British intelligence let a dead body carrying fake invasion plans wash up on the Spanish coast, convincing Hitler the Allies would land in Greece. Which Mediterranean island was the real target?
source_excerpt: the discovered Anglo-Saxon order confirms the assumption that the planned attacks will be directed mainly against Sardinia and the Peloponnesus.

extra.why_interesting: The scheme sounds too absurd to have worked; players can reason from the 1943 Mediterranean timeline to the real target.
extra.verification_notes: Operation Mincemeat deceived Germany about the Allied target; the real invasion target was Sicily (Operation Husky), per Wikipedia.

explanation: Operation Mincemeat worked so well that German forces were shifted toward Greece and Sardinia, and the Allied landing on Sicily that July met weaker resistance than expected.

question: The Molotov cocktail got its name as a joke at the expense of the Soviet foreign minister. Soldiers of which country coined it while fighting the Red Army in the winter of 1939 to 1940?
source_excerpt: The name 'Molotov cocktail' was coined by the Finns during the Winter War in 1939.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the weapon was named by or for the Soviets; it was in fact a joke at Molotov's expense by the small country he was attacking.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Finns coined the name during the Winter War as mockery of Molotov.

explanation: Molotov claimed Soviet planes were dropping food to starving Finns, so the Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets and offered a drink to go with them.

question: Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park built on an earlier breakthrough: mathematicians from which country first cracked the German Enigma cipher, back in 1932?
source_excerpt: In December 1932, Marian Rejewski made what historian David Kahn describes as one of the greatest advances in cryptologic history, by applying pure mathematics

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone credits Alan Turing and Bletchley Park with cracking Enigma. The player starts from Britain and has to remember that a different country's mathematicians had already broken it years before the war even started.
extra.verification_notes: Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski first broke military Enigma in December 1932, as stated on Wikipedia's Cipher Bureau (Poland) page.

explanation: Marian Rejewski and his colleagues at the Polish Cipher Bureau reconstructed the Enigma machine with pure mathematics, and in July 1939 Poland handed its methods and replica machines to Britain and France, giving Bletchley Park a seven-year head start.

question: Germany made its very last reparations payment for the First World War in which year?
source_excerpt: The final payment was made on 3 October 2010, settling German loan debts in regard to reparations.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes reparations were a 1920s and 1930s story that Hitler simply cancelled. The answer lands in the age of smartphones, decades after the last trench was filled in.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the final payment settling WWI reparation-related loan debts was made on 3 October 2010; no newer event supersedes it.

explanation: Hitler stopped payments in 1933, but West Germany took the debt back on in 1953 and agreed that interest on some bonds would wait until the country was reunified. That final bill of around seventy million euros was paid on 3 October 2010, exactly twenty years after reunification.
